concept.technique_name: smart numbers plug-in for regular figures

examples.problem_statement: The circumference of a circle is 7/8 the perimeter of a square. Quantity A: the area of the square. Quantity B: the area of the circle. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.description: Note that all squares are in proportion to all other squares and all circles to all other circles, and the two figures are tied by a fixed relation, so a single set of plugged-in values settles the comparison. Pick the value for the square — choosing the circle's radius first would drag \pi into every square calculation.
Turn the chosen side into the square's perimeter, since the perimeter is what the given 7/8 relationship refers to.
Square the chosen side to get the area of the square, which is Quantity A.
Apply the given relationship to the perimeter found in step 2 to get the circle's circumference.
Set the circumference formula equal to 7 and solve for the radius, the quantity the circle's area needs.

solution.result: Quantity B is smaller than 4, so Quantity A is larger
solution.description: Square the radius from step 5 in the circle-area formula and evaluate it on the calculator with 3.14 for \pi, then compare that value against the square's area of 4.

key_reminders: A square's perimeter is 4s and its area is s^2.
A circle's circumference is 2\pi r and its area is \pi r^2.
Squares are all similar to one another and circles are all similar to one another, so when the two are locked in a fixed ratio, one plug-in gives the answer for every case.
common_mistakes: Plugging in the circle first (e.g. r = 2, C = 4\pi), which forces the square's perimeter to 32\pi/7 and leaves \pi in the square's area — awkward rather than wrong.
Assuming the 7/8 ratio of circumference to perimeter carries over to a 7/8 ratio of areas.

concept.technique_name: chained ratio scaled by a known difference

examples.problem_statement: The ratio of Jim's salary for October to his salary for November was 9 : 8 and the ratio of the salary for November to that for December was 3 : 4. The worker got 40 rupees more for December than for October and received a bonus constituting 40 per cent of the salary for three months. Find the bonus. (Assume that the number of workdays is the same in every month.)

solution.description: Join the two ratios on their shared November term so all three months sit on one scale; November stays at 8, which sends December's 4 up to 10.666.

solution.result: 1.666 ratio units correspond to the 40 rupee gap
solution.description: Subtract October's share from December's on that common scale, because the problem tells you what this particular gap is worth in rupees.
Divide the 40 rupees across the 1.666 units from step 2 to get the value of a single unit, the scale factor for everything else.
Add the three monthly shares, since the bonus is a percentage of the salary for all three months together.
Convert the three-month total into rupees with the step 3 unit value and take 40 per cent of it to get the bonus.

key_reminders: Two ratios sharing a term combine into one chain by holding that shared term fixed.
A stated difference in real money fixes the value of one ratio unit.
40 per cent is applied as the multiplier 0.4.
common_mistakes: Treating the 40 rupees as the value of one ratio unit instead of the 1.666-unit gap between December and October.
Combining 9 : 8 with 3 : 4 without first making November agree, which corrupts December's share.

concept.technique_name: logarithm of a power of the base

solution.result: the argument is rewritten as a power of 10
solution.description: Rewrite the decimal as a power of the base 10 so the logarithm's argument matches its base.

solution.result: the exponent moves out in front
solution.description: Bring the exponent from step 1 down as a coefficient using the power rule for logarithms.
Replace \log_{10}10 with 1 since any log of its own base is 1, and multiply out.

common_mistakes: Reporting 4 instead of -4 by counting the four decimal places and dropping the negative sign on the exponent.

concept.technique_name: ordering constraints bounding a variable's placement

examples.problem_statement: Exactly six piano classes are given sequentially on Monday: two with more than one student and four with exactly one student. Exactly four females — Gimena, Holly, Iyanna, and Kate — and five males — Leung, Nate, Oscar, Pedro, and Saul — attend these classes. Each student attends exactly one class. The following must obtain: Iyanna and Leung together constitute one class. Pedro and exactly two others together constitute one class. Kate is the first female, but not the first student, to attend a class. Gimena's class is at some time after Iyanna's but at some time before Pedro's. Oscar's class is at some time after Gimena's. Question: Which one of the following is a complete and accurate list of classes any one of which could be the class Gimena attends? (A) the fourth, the fifth (B) the fourth, the sixth (C) the second, the fourth, the fifth (D) the third, the fifth, the sixth (E) the second, the third, the fourth

solution.result: three separate classes must sit ahead of Gimena's
solution.description: Collect the groups forced earlier than Gimena: the opening N/S slot, Kate's class, and the Iyanna-Leung class each has to come before her.

solution.result: Gimena's earliest possible class is the fourth
solution.description: Count the three classes from step 1 as occupying the first three slots, which pushes Gimena no earlier than the fourth class.

solution.result: Gimena cannot attend the last class
solution.description: Use the rule that Pedro's class follows Gimena's — something must come after her, so the sixth class is unavailable to her.

solution.result: the fourth and the fifth, which is choice (A)
solution.description: Combine the floor from step 2 with the ceiling from step 3 and match the surviving pair of classes against the answer choices.

key_reminders: Each group that must precede a variable consumes one earlier slot, setting a floor on that variable's position.
A variable that must be followed by another cannot occupy the final slot.
common_mistakes: Counting only Iyanna-Leung as preceding Gimena and letting her sit third, which is what makes choices (D) and (E) tempting.
Forgetting that Pedro comes after Gimena and admitting the sixth class, as in choice (B).
